title: How to Bless Your Home and Your Children
excerpt: Speaking blessing over your children is not superstition. It is a parent doing what God has always done: naming a person, and speaking a good future over them out loud.
body:
Most parents speak constant correction over their children and almost never speak blessing. We tell them what they did wrong, what to fix, what to stop. The flow of words runs one way, toward improvement. And then we wonder why a child grows up unsure whether they are delighted in. They heard plenty about their faults. They rarely heard, in words, that they were loved and wanted and meant for good.

Blessing is the practice of speaking good over a person on purpose. It is not flattery and it is not a wish. It is a parent standing in their God-given authority over a child and naming who they are and the good God intends for them. The Bible is full of it, and our homes are largely empty of it, and the gap shapes a generation.

## Why words spoken over a child matter

The blessing runs deep in Scripture. Aaron and his sons were commanded to bless Israel with specific words: "The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the Lord lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace." Jacob blessed his sons on his deathbed, each one by name, with words that marked their futures. Parents laid hands on children and spoke over them, and it was understood that the words did something.

We have grown skittish about this, suspicious that it sounds like magic. It is not magic. It is the simple, weighty truth that words have power, that a child becomes in part what they are repeatedly told they are, and that a parent's voice carries authority a child's soul records and keeps. When God made the world, he did it with words. When a parent blesses a child, they image that same creative speech, calling forth in words the good they long to see.

## How to bless your children

Keep it simple and make it physical. Lay a hand on the child's head or shoulder, look at them, and speak. The touch matters. It says this is for you, particularly, not a general sentiment cast into the air.

Use the old words when you want a frame: "The Lord bless you and keep you." The words of Numbers 6 have been spoken over children for thousands of years, and there is weight in joining that long line. Then add the particular. Name the child. Name a good thing you see in them and a good future you long for. "May you grow strong and kind. May you love what is true. May the Lord make his face shine on you all your days."

Do it at a regular hinge of the day so it becomes a rhythm and not an event. Bedtime is natural. The door before school is good. Birthdays especially, when you bless the year ahead. The repetition is what lodges it. A blessing spoken once is a nice moment. A blessing spoken every night becomes the soundtrack a child hears in their own head for the rest of their life.

## Bless the home, too

A home can be marked as God's ground, set apart on purpose for what happens inside it. This is not about chasing away spirits with a ritual. It is about a household declaring, out loud, whose this house is and what it is for. When you move into a place, gather and pray through it, room by room if you like, asking that this be a house of peace, of welcome, of truth, a place where God is known. When the family has come through a hard stretch, or a new season begins, say it again.

The point is intention. A home is formed by what is honored in it, and a family that names its house as belonging to God, repeatedly and out loud, is a family pointing its whole common life in one direction.

## Bless even when you do not feel it

The hard nights are the important ones. The night the child was defiant and you are still angry, the night you are exhausted and have nothing tender left, these are exactly the nights to bless anyway. The blessing is not a reward for good behavior, and it is not contingent on your mood. It is a declaration of who the child is and whose they are, which does not change because the day was bad. A child who is blessed even on the night they failed learns that they are loved underneath their performance, which is the gospel itself in miniature.

I have skipped the blessing on the angry nights, withholding it as if it were owed only to the deserving. That was wrong. Those were the nights my children most needed to hear that the love did not move. Grace that only arrives when behavior is good is not grace at all.

## This week

Tonight, lay your hand on your child's head and speak a blessing over them out loud. Use the words of Numbers 6 if you need a frame, then name them and name a good future. Do it again tomorrow, at the same hinge of the day, until it becomes the thing you simply do. On the hard nights, do it anyway, especially then.

Your children are going to carry a voice in their heads about who they are. Make sure some of that voice is yours, and make sure it is good.
